meta.title: Down the Mississippi River, an altered wetland landscape faces new threats

footer.about: This is part of “Down the Drain: A watershed moment for America's greatest wetlands." Reporters from news organizations across the Mississippi River basin investigated the benefits of wetlands, and the increasing threats in the wake of a 2023 U.S. Supreme Court decision that removed protections from a large share of these crucial landscapes. Mississippi River Basin Ag & Water Desk reporters from ten states investigated wetlands issues including the changing legal landscape for wetlands protections, shifting protections to states; how the "Swampbuster" rule is being challenged by an Iowa farmer; how one coastal wetland is growing and bucking the trend; the role of duck hunting in conservation, and how a burgeoning mitigation business could collapse without federal regulations.

content.value: Before the American expansion west in the 19th century, the Mississippi River was a landscape of wetlands. Its northern tributaries coursed through prairie potholes and peatland bogs in the upper Midwest. Massive marshes and wet prairies sprawled from Ohio through Indiana, Illinois and Iowa. The confluence of the Ohio and Mississippi rivers marked the beginning of a swamp forest dominated by cypress, nearly 24 million acres that spread out into Arkansas, Mississippi and Louisiana. The river split into a web of distributaries in Louisiana, creating a bayou and coastal marsh region of unparalleled biological productivity bordering the Gulf of Mexico. Two centuries of alteration through logging, levee building, ditch digging, channelization and tile drains have converted many of those landscapes into the nation’s corn belt. By the time the value of wetlands had been recognized and some protections extended in the 20th century, states such as Iowa, Illinois and Arkansas lost 80% or more of their wetlands. Flood control engineering of the lower Mississippi River has consumed Louisiana’s coast and threatens to take Cajun culture and the nation’s seafood supply with it.

Starting in the early 1900s, duck hunters and nature lovers succeeded in changing attitudes about wetlands and promoted federal policies that have preserved and restored millions of acres. That’s crucial for the Mississippi Flyway, the nation’s largest migratory bird corridor. 

A 2023 U.S. Supreme Court decision removed federal protection from a large number of the nation’s wetlands. That’s left their fate in the hands of the states, which have sharply varying policies. Some worry that a new era of wetland destruction awaits.

A wetland tour of the Mississippi River basin illustrates both the damage done — and what’s left to save.

slides.text: Some of the largest surviving wetlands are peat bogs, unique and delicate ecosystems, mainly in Minnesota, which didn’t respond well to the drainage techniques that were used by prairie farmers. More recently, scientists have recognized their benefit in storing carbon and fostering biodiversity. Minnesota peat bogs

component.caption: A tamarack bog in Hennepin County, Minnesota.
component.credit: James Eli Shiffer/The Minnesota Star Tribune

slides.text: Covering 33,000 acres in Wisconsin farm country, Horicon Marsh is a remnant of the Ice Age. It was dammed and ditched for farming and milling, but in the 1920s became one of the first wetland restoration projects. Extent of the Horicon Marsh

component.caption: A duck hunter on the Horicon Marsh in 2015.

slides.text: The prairie pothole region that stretches from Iowa, Minnesota, the Dakotas and into Canada has seen some of the most widespread conversion into farmland. In a part of north central Iowa once known as the “thousand-lake” region, Cairo Lake was drained around the turn of the 20th century. Its outlines are still visible among row crops. Approximate outline of Cairo Lake

American migrants heading west found their horses sinking into the muck of saturated grasslands or “wet prairies.” The Grand Prairie covered almost 16 counties in Illinois. Its drainage created some of the most fertile farmland in America, but also contributed to Illinois losing at least 85% of its wetlands. Extent of the Grand Prairie

component.caption: "Flight of toads, mosquitoes and lobsters following drainage," a fanciful illustration in the Drainage Journal in 1888.

slides.text: Similarly, the Grand Kankakee Marsh was so huge that some called it the “Everglades of the North,” as presidents and princes came to hunt there, its bounty supplying Chicago restaurants. Then the Kankakee River was straightened and the state’s largest lake ditched. There’s almost no trace left. Approximate area of the former Kankakee Marsh

component.caption: A vintage view of the Grand Kankakee Marsh, a mecca for waterfowl hunters.
component.credit: Courtesy of the Kankakee Valley Historical Society

slides.text: An immense cypress forest used to spread over nearly 24 million acres of floodplain south of Illinois until most was logged and contained by levees and ditches. One part of that was Big Swamp in the Missouri Bootheel, now almost completely converted to farm fields. Missouri Bootheel

component.caption: The Missouri Bootheel is depicted as almost unbroken swamp in 1857.
component.credit: Courtesy of the State Historical Society of Missouri

slides.text: The massive and unmistakable ivory-billed woodpecker thrived in the lower basin’s swamps, but runaway logging destroyed its habitat and the bird was only known to survive in one patch of northeast Louisiana woods, called the Singer Tract. The tract, which was also logged, is now part of the Tensas River National Wildlife Refuge. The last known sighting of the ivory-bill was there in 1944. It was declared extinct in 2022. Tensas River National Wildlife Refuge

component.caption: An ivory-billed woodpecker in its final known wild home, the Singer Tract, in 1937.
component.credit: James T. Tanner, via U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service

slides.text: Covering more than a million acres of south Louisiana, the Atchafalaya Basin is the nation’s largest river swamp, a habitat for migratory waterfowl and crucial to Louisiana’s seafood economy and Cajun culture. Protected by federal engineers as a flood outlet, its delta is one of the only areas of the state’s coast that’s growing. Atchafalaya River

component.caption: One of the many channels that wind through the Atchafalaya River basin in Iberville Parish, Louisiana, shown in February 2025.
component.credit: James Eli Shiffer/The Minnesota Star Tribune

slides.text: The wetlands of the Louisiana gulf coast provide a bounty of oysters, shrimp and other seafood, yet are also the site of one of the world’s biggest environmental catastrophes. A hundred years of river sediment cutoff, sea level rise and channels dug by oil companies have caused 2,000 square miles of the coast to wash away; estimates show a loss of a football field of land every 100 minutes.

component.caption: The erosion of Bayou Bienvenue's marshland makes New Orleans more vulnerable to storm surge from hurricanes.
component.credit: James Eli Shiffer/The Minnesota Star Tribune

slides.text: All told, more than half of U.S. wetlands have been drained, filled or altered. In the 1780s, before widespread development and agricultural expansion, the estimated extent of wetlands was about 221 million acres, an area that would have stretched from northwest Nebraska to southeast Kentucky. Two centuries later, a 1990 estimate of remaining wetlands was about 103 million acres. Equivalent area of 1780s wetlands Equivalent area of 1980s wetlands
